disclaimer: An independent student guide. Programme facts link to official sources; the workflow, checklists, topic prompts and practical advice are authored suggestions. Your cohort's EU-HEM Thesis Guidelines and your thesis university's instructions govern approval, supervision, ethics, assessment and deadlines. Topic prompts are illustrative questions, not approved or available projects.

facts.title: 120 ECTS across two years
facts.text: EU-HEM is a four-semester master's programme worth 120 ECTS. The fourth semester is dedicated to the master's thesis; the published Bologna curriculum assigns it 30 ECTS.

facts.title: A thesis connected to your track
facts.text: Write the thesis at one of the two universities of your selected track. Use the host options in My thesis to see your current cohort's pair; confirm your host and its procedures with the programme.

facts.title: Your own scientific investigation
facts.text: The thesis concerns your specialisation and involves individual research, clear reporting and discussion. Ideas may originate with you, lecturers or an external public or private organisation; a promising idea still needs supervision and approval.

facts.title: Get the current cohort's guidelines
facts.text: Bologna directs EU-HEM students to the joint Thesis Guidelines circulated annually before summer. Partner universities use shared evaluation criteria. Obtain that year's document and host instructions before treating any planning date or format as official.

facts.title: Use the Summer School to prepare
facts.text: The programme's Summer School at the end of Semester 2 includes thesis preparation and a thesis workshop. Use it to test your question, approach and project organisation; check the current event arrangements.

journey.label: Notice what interests you
journey.goal: Build a small research notebook while you learn, without committing to a project too early.
actions: Keep a list of problems that interest you in health economics, management, policy or population health.
For each idea, save one useful paper and note which decision, population and setting it concerns.
Compare track content with the skills your questions would need: modelling, policy analysis, organisation or public health.
journey.deliverable: Three topic seeds, each explained in two sentences.
journey.pitfall: Choosing a fashionable title before knowing what question you could answer.

checklist.text: I have recorded three research interests.
I have read an initial paper for each interest.
I have linked my interests to track skills.

journey.label: Turn an interest into a question
journey.goal: Move from a broad theme to one question with plausible evidence and supervision.
actions: Read recent reviews, identify an unresolved issue and draft two alternative research questions.
Check the data or document sources before promising a quantitative analysis or interviews.
Identify potential supervisors through the host's official process, course themes and staff research interests; prepare a short concept note.
journey.deliverable: A one-page concept note: question, relevance, proposed method, evidence and constraints.
journey.pitfall: Assuming an internship, company contact or interesting dataset automatically becomes an approved thesis.

checklist.text: I can state my main question in one sentence.
I have checked a plausible evidence source.
I know how my possible host allocates supervisors.

journey.label: Test the plan before Year 2
journey.goal: Use the circulated guidelines and thesis preparation activities to check feasibility.
actions: Obtain the current joint Thesis Guidelines; record the host's real approval, registration, submission and defence requirements.
Bring your concept note to thesis preparation discussions and ask what would make the question too ambitious.
Confirm what you can access, who can supervise and what your alternative is if access or recruitment fails.
journey.deliverable: A revised concept note and a list of requirements to confirm.
journey.pitfall: Using dates or word limits from an older student or archive as current rules.

checklist.text: I have the current cohort's Thesis Guidelines.
I have checked host procedures and official dates.
I have a realistic alternative if access fails.

journey.label: Agree a feasible project
journey.goal: Agree the scope, method, responsibilities and permissions before substantive work begins.
actions: Agree a supervisor, precise question and proposal through the required local process.
Check variables, sample or document coverage, software skills and the time available. Pilot a small analysis or search with permitted material.
Determine ethics, consent, data protection and access requirements with your host and supervisor before recruitment, collection or controlled-data use.
journey.deliverable: An agreed proposal, access plan and schedule with a buffer.
journey.pitfall: Starting participant recruitment or handling restricted data before the required decisions and permissions.

checklist.text: My question, scope and method have been agreed.
Data access or evidence availability is confirmed.
Required ethics and data permissions have been determined.
My work and feedback schedule includes a buffer.

journey.label: Research, write and revise
journey.goal: Produce a transparent, defensible answer to the agreed question.
actions: Keep a research log and organised, backed-up versions of permitted data, code, notes and drafts.
Write the methods as you work; send focused drafts and specific questions at the agreed feedback points.
Explain uncertainty, alternative interpretations and limitations. Re-run checks and revise claims when the evidence requires it.
journey.deliverable: A complete draft with a traceable chain from question to evidence to conclusion.
journey.pitfall: Leaving writing until analysis is finished, or adding methods that do not help answer the question.

checklist.text: My research decisions and materials are documented.
I have received feedback on a complete draft.
I have checked results, references and limitations.

journey.label: Submit and explain your contribution
journey.when: Your host's confirmed submission and defence window
journey.goal: Meet the actual submission requirements and explain the work confidently.
actions: Check registration, eligibility, upload format, declarations, confidentiality arrangements and the defence procedure against current instructions.
Explain the question, why the design fits, your main finding and the strongest limitation in a short presentation; use the host's prescribed length.
Practise questions about validity, assumptions, originality and implications. Save proof of submission and check the uploaded file.
journey.deliverable: A verified submission and a clear account of your contribution.
journey.pitfall: Treating a local checklist as proof that the university has accepted the thesis.

checklist.text: Official submission and defence requirements are confirmed.
The submitted file and receipt have been checked.
I can explain my findings and limitations without reading a script.

topics.title: When does a screening strategy offer value?
topics.question: Under which uptake and cost assumptions could one defined screening strategy be cost-effective compared with usual care in a chosen health system?
topics.dataIdea: Published effectiveness, cost and quality-of-life estimates for one condition; confirm comparable populations and a justified payer or societal perspective.
topics.feasibility: Begin with a transparent decision tree where clinically appropriate. A complex lifetime model may exceed your available time or evidence; test uncertainty rather than presenting one definitive ratio.

topics.title: Can a service afford a new technology?
topics.question: How would introducing a specified remote-monitoring service affect a payer's annual budget under alternative eligible-population and adoption assumptions?
topics.dataIdea: Published unit costs, eligible-population estimates and service-use evidence; partner estimates only if authorised and documented.
topics.feasibility: Specify the budget holder and horizon. Budget impact and cost-effectiveness answer different questions; show adoption scenarios and identify uncertain inputs.

topics.title: Which utility estimates support a model?
topics.question: How comparable are published health-state utility estimates used in economic evaluations of one defined chronic condition?
topics.dataIdea: Peer-reviewed utility studies and economic evaluations with explicit eligibility criteria, instruments and population characteristics.
topics.feasibility: Scope the condition and years before searching. Differences in instrument, valuation country and severity may prevent pooling; a structured comparison can still be useful.

topics.title: Financial protection and unmet care
topics.question: How have out-of-pocket spending and reported unmet healthcare need varied across a small set of comparable European health systems over a defined period?
topics.dataIdea: OECD spending aggregates and Eurostat unmet-need indicators; first verify country coverage, definitions and available years.
topics.feasibility: Use consistent units, definitions and denominators. Country-level association cannot establish that an individual's spending caused unmet need; explain ecological and comparability limits.

topics.title: Did a defined policy change an outcome?
topics.question: Did one documented change in healthcare eligibility coincide with a change in utilisation relative to a defensible comparison population?
topics.dataIdea: A verified reform timeline and accessible observations before and after implementation for affected and comparison groups.
topics.feasibility: A causal claim needs a credible identification strategy, not just a before-and-after graph. Check pre-trends, concurrent reforms and spillovers; use a descriptive policy study if the design cannot be supported.

topics.title: How do reimbursement systems differ?
topics.question: How do two selected countries incorporate clinical evidence, economic evidence and uncertainty into reimbursement decisions for a defined technology category?
topics.dataIdea: Public assessment manuals, decision documents and legislation with a documented search and a common comparison framework.
topics.feasibility: Choose comparable institutions and a manageable period. Published documents reveal formal procedures; they may not capture informal decision-making or implementation.

topics.title: Capacity and hospital performance
topics.question: How have selected measures of hospital capacity and service use changed in comparable regions or health systems over a defined period?
topics.dataIdea: Public aggregate workforce, bed and utilisation indicators from OECD or Eurostat; local waiting-time series only where accessible and comparable.
topics.feasibility: Avoid interpreting more beds or shorter stays as automatically better performance. Case mix, definitions and service substitution matter; aggregates cannot identify individual hospital processes.

topics.title: What helps a digital service become routine?
topics.question: Which organisational barriers and facilitators shape implementation of one remote-care service in a defined healthcare setting?
topics.dataIdea: Approved interviews with relevant staff, if access and required review are confirmed; a document-based case or evidence review is a possible alternative.
topics.feasibility: Recruitment and transcription take time. Select a clear analytic framework, protect participants' identities and avoid treating a small convenience sample as representative of all institutions.

topics.title: How do institutions use quality indicators?
topics.question: How do two healthcare organisations describe the use of patient-experience or quality indicators in service improvement?
topics.dataIdea: Public annual reports, quality strategies and documented improvement programmes; internal dashboards require specific permission.
topics.feasibility: Use explicit case-selection and coding rules. Public reports may emphasise success; separate reported intentions from demonstrated effects on care.

topics.title: Who is missing preventive care?
topics.question: How does uptake of one preventive service differ across available socioeconomic groups in selected European countries?
topics.dataIdea: Public Eurostat health-survey tabulations and published survey metadata; confirm the required breakdown is released before choosing the exact population.
topics.feasibility: Check age eligibility, survey weights and uncertainty in reported estimates. Aggregate tabulations may support a disparity description but not individual-level adjustment or causal explanation.

topics.title: Coverage gains and financial hardship
topics.question: How have health-service coverage and financial-protection indicators evolved in a small group of comparable countries?
topics.dataIdea: WHO and World Bank public indicators with attention to reference years, estimation methods and missing values.
topics.feasibility: Some indicators are modelled or measured in infrequent surveys. Avoid inventing annual observations or claiming that an observed national trend proves a programme's impact.

topics.title: Who coordinates prevention across sectors?
topics.question: How do two local or national prevention strategies assign responsibilities across health services, education and community organisations?
topics.dataIdea: Public strategy documents, implementation reports and evaluation studies; approved stakeholder interviews could complement the document analysis.
topics.feasibility: Define the preventive issue and levels of governance. Stated responsibilities are not evidence that coordination works; look for implementation evidence and document its absence.

methods.name: Descriptive quantitative analysis
methods.bestFor: Measuring patterns, differences or associations in accessible observations.
requirements: An operational definition of each outcome and exposure
A plan for missingness, uncertainty and relevant confounding
methods.strength: A focused analysis can make important health-system patterns visible and reproducible.
methods.limits: Regression does not automatically remove bias. Individual conclusions cannot be inferred from country aggregates, and association alone does not identify a causal effect.
methods.questionExample: How does reported unmet care vary by income group?

methods.name: Policy evaluation & causal designs
methods.bestFor: Estimating a policy or intervention effect when a credible comparison is available.
requirements: A precisely timed intervention and defined affected population
An explicit counterfactual and identification assumptions
Suitable pre/post observations and robustness checks
methods.strength: A defensible design can separate a treatment effect from some competing explanations.
methods.limits: Difference-in-differences needs a defensible parallel-trends assumption; interrupted time series needs adequate observations and attention to other changes. Discuss threats rather than treating a method name as proof.
methods.questionExample: Did an eligibility reform change service use relative to a comparable group?

methods.name: Economic evaluation & modelling
methods.bestFor: Comparing the costs and consequences of specified alternatives for a decision-maker.
requirements: A justified perspective, comparator, population and time horizon
Traceable effectiveness, resource-use and valuation inputs
A model structure suited to the clinical pathway and an uncertainty plan
methods.strength: Makes trade-offs and assumptions explicit and tests how a decision changes under uncertainty.
methods.limits: A precise-looking result can conceal weak inputs or inappropriate structure. Cost-effectiveness, budget impact and affordability are distinct questions; use reporting guidance alongside sound design.
methods.questionExample: Under what assumptions could a screening strategy offer good value?

methods.name: Structured evidence review
methods.bestFor: Synthesising a defined body of evidence or mapping what is known about a question.
requirements: A protocol with eligibility criteria and documented searches
A transparent screening and extraction process
An appraisal and synthesis approach matched to the review purpose
methods.strength: Clarifies evidence gaps, conflicting findings and whether results are transferable.
methods.limits: A systematic review and a scoping review serve different purposes. PRISMA supports transparent reporting; completing a checklist does not establish methodological quality or make a narrative review systematic.
methods.questionExample: Which utility estimates are available for a defined condition, and how comparable are they?

methods.name: Qualitative interviews
methods.bestFor: Understanding experiences, mechanisms and implementation in a defined context.
requirements: Required ethics, informed-consent and data-handling arrangements
An interview guide and transparent coding or thematic-analysis plan
methods.strength: Can explain how participants understand a process and why implementation succeeds or struggles.
methods.limits: Access, transcription and interpretation require time. Protect confidentiality, reflect on your role and avoid numerical generalisation from a small purposive sample.
methods.questionExample: What barriers do staff report when introducing a remote-care service?

methods.name: Comparative policy & document analysis
methods.bestFor: Comparing formal policies, governance arrangements or institutional approaches.
requirements: A justified set of cases and a common analytic framework
Attention to source purpose, missing voices and implementation evidence
methods.strength: Often permits a feasible project with public documents and a clearly bounded comparison.
methods.limits: Written policy is not necessarily implemented practice. Language differences, selective publication and case selection can distort a comparison.
methods.questionExample: How do two reimbursement agencies handle uncertainty in technology assessments?

supervision.intro: Find a good match between your question, method and a supervisor's expertise. Your host's allocation or approval process takes priority over informal contact.
find: Check the official supervisor process and whether you may approach staff directly.
Read staff research profiles and one relevant paper; explain the specific connection to your question.
Send a concise concept note and ask about fit, availability and the appropriate next step. Avoid a generic message to many people.
supervision.emailTemplate:
Subject: EU-HEM thesis enquiry — [focused topic]

Dear [title and name],
I am an EU-HEM student in the [track] track, considering my thesis at [host university]. Your work on [specific paper or theme] connects with my proposed question: [one sentence].

I am considering [method] using [evidence source]. I have checked [access or feasibility point], and my main uncertainty is [specific issue]. I have attached a short concept note.

If the local process permits direct enquiries, would this fit your expertise and availability, or could you suggest the appropriate next step?

Best regards,
[Name]
meeting: Send the draft or agenda in the agreed format with enough reading time.
Bring a small number of decisions: question, design, interpretation or scope; explain what you have already tried.
After the meeting, record agreed actions, responsibilities and the next feedback point.
expectations: Agree meeting frequency, response times, draft milestones and who approves changes.
Clarify how an external organisation and university supervisor will divide responsibilities.
Keep ownership of the research and writing; supervision supports decisions rather than replacing them.

sections.title: From a broad theme to an answerable question
sections.intro: A thesis becomes manageable when the question determines the evidence and method.

items.title: Start with a decision or problem
items.text: Replace 'digital health' with a decision someone faces: which service, for whom, in which setting and with which outcome? Explain who would benefit from an answer.

items.title: State the boundaries
items.text: Define the population, intervention or exposure, comparator where relevant, outcome, setting and period. These prompts help specify a question; not every qualitative or policy study needs an intervention-style PICO format.

items.title: Make the claim match the design
items.text: Choose whether you are describing, comparing, explaining experiences, synthesising evidence or estimating a causal effect. Use 'associated with' when the design cannot identify causation.

items.title: Find a modest contribution
items.text: A new context, updated evidence, clearer comparison or transparent sensitivity analysis can be valuable. You do not need to solve an entire health-system problem.

items.title: Run a feasibility test
items.text: Can you access the necessary evidence, use the required method, obtain permissions and finish within your actual schedule? Specify a smaller alternative before relying on uncertain access.

sections.title: Read strategically and build an evidence map
sections.intro: Read to sharpen the question and design, then maintain a traceable record.

items.title: Begin with orientation
items.text: Use recent reviews and key papers to identify terms, theories, debates and common methods. Follow citations in both directions and search more than one relevant source.

items.title: Create a literature matrix
items.text: For each paper record the question, setting, data, method, finding, limitation and relevance to your study. This makes differences visible and prevents a chapter that only lists summaries.

items.title: Record the search
items.text: Save databases, search strings, dates and eligibility decisions. If conducting a systematic or scoping review, agree a protocol and the appropriate reporting guidance before screening.

items.title: Check the original source
items.text: Read the paper behind a claim, verify bibliographic details and distinguish evidence from opinion. A reference manager helps organisation but does not verify that a citation supports your sentence.

sections.title: Evidence, access, ethics and integrity
sections.intro: Confirm what you are allowed to do before collecting or using material. Public availability, ethics and permission are separate questions.

items.title: Public aggregates are a useful starting point
items.text: OECD, Eurostat, WHO and World Bank portals provide health indicators. Check metadata, missing years, definitions, units, licence and revisions. A portal link does not guarantee the variables, subgroup detail or individual records your question needs.

items.title: Controlled data need an access plan
items.text: Hospital records, registries, survey microdata and internal company material may require applications, contracts and a secure environment. Written permission and realistic access time matter; removing names alone does not guarantee anonymity.

items.title: Ask for an ethics determination early
items.text: Your host and faculty decide what review or exemption applies. Erasmus explicitly notes that faculties determine review needs for educational student research. Obtain the required decision before recruitment, collection or relevant data use; public or secondary data are not a universal exemption.

items.title: Protect people and confidential information
items.text: Agree consent, minimum necessary data, storage, retention and sharing arrangements. Do not place participant identifiers or confidential institutional material in this public hub or an unapproved external tool.

items.title: Keep the work reproducible
items.text: Preserve permitted raw inputs separately from cleaned versions, document transformations and organise code or extraction tables. Record exclusions and analytic changes; report inconvenient or null results honestly.

items.title: Check the actual AI policy
items.text: Ask which uses are permitted by your host, assessment rules and supervisor. Bologna's guidance for assessed work requires attention to teacher instructions, critical verification and disclosure. That is a local example, not joint permission for every EU-HEM thesis. Never invent references, observations or analysis.

sections.title: Build the proposal and write alongside the research
sections.intro: Use this outline as a starting point, then follow the actual host template and length requirements.

items.title: Proposal: the compact argument
items.text: Working title; problem and relevance; focused question; short evidence gap; design and method; evidence and access; ethics and integrity considerations; expected contribution; limitations; schedule and initial references.

items.title: Introduction and literature
items.text: Explain the problem, what is established, what remains uncertain and exactly what you will examine. Link the research question to a conceptual framework instead of collecting unrelated background.

items.title: Methods
items.text: Describe case or sample selection, data, definitions, procedures, analysis, assumptions and required permissions clearly enough that a reader can understand and evaluate what you did.

items.title: Results
items.text: Present findings in a logical order linked to the question. Use readable tables and figures with units, denominators and uncertainty. Separate observations from interpretation.

items.title: Discussion and conclusion
items.text: Answer the question, compare with previous evidence, explain limitations and justified implications. Do not turn an association into a policy effect or generalise beyond the study population.

items.title: Revise with purpose
items.text: Start with the logic and evidence, then structure, then wording and formatting. Write an abstract after the core argument stabilises. Check that every conclusion is supported and every borrowed idea is cited.

sections.title: Finish well: submission and defence
sections.intro: Use a final checklist, while verifying every administrative requirement with your actual thesis host.

items.title: Confirm the administrative route
items.text: Record the official thesis registration, graduation application, eligibility, submission and defence dates as separate items. Check required forms, examiner arrangements and any supervisor approval; this hub does not submit them for you.

items.title: Check the final file
items.text: Verify title and author details, abstract, figures, references, appendices, declarations, file format and any accessibility requirements. Open the uploaded version and retain the receipt.

items.title: Resolve confidentiality before uploading
items.text: Agree what may appear in the assessed thesis, defence and public repository. Ask about embargo or redaction procedures when material is confidential; do not promise publication to an external partner without agreement.

items.title: Practise the research story
items.text: Explain the problem, question, design, key result, contribution and strongest limitation. Use a small number of figures that advance the argument and respect the official presentation length.

items.title: Prepare to defend decisions
items.text: Practise why you chose the method, which assumptions matter, what could bias the result and how a different design might help. Acknowledge uncertainty directly; it demonstrates understanding.

sprint.title: A suggested 12-week research rhythm
sprint.disclaimer: An adaptable work example, not an official thesis duration or deadline. Start earlier for access, ethics or recruitment; account for your host's calendar, supervisor availability and a submission buffer.

weeks.label: Weeks 1–2
weeks.focus: Agree the question, scope and design; confirm evidence and permissions. Revise the schedule if access is unresolved.
weeks.deliverable: Agreed plan and a feasible evidence route.

weeks.label: Weeks 3–4
weeks.focus: Build the literature matrix, pilot extraction or analysis and draft the methods. Begin collection only after required permissions.
weeks.deliverable: Pilot results, organised material and a methods draft.

weeks.label: Weeks 5–6
weeks.focus: Complete the main collection or extraction and perform the core analysis. Record decisions and resolve major problems with your supervisor.
weeks.deliverable: Initial findings and a documented analysis trail.

weeks.label: Weeks 7–8
weeks.focus: Check assumptions, sensitivity or interpretation; draft results and discussion alongside the introduction.
weeks.deliverable: A coherent full draft for scheduled feedback.

weeks.label: Weeks 9–10
weeks.focus: Address feedback, re-check claims and references, and improve figures, limitations and the abstract.
weeks.deliverable: A revised draft and a completed reporting check.

weeks.label: Weeks 11–12
weeks.focus: Use the buffer for corrections, final administrative checks and defence practice. Submit only against confirmed official dates.
weeks.deliverable: Verified submission materials and a rehearsed presentation.

faq.question: When should I start thinking about my thesis?
faq.answer: Keep an interest notebook in Semester 1, investigate questions and supervision in Semester 2, and use the summer preparation activities. Aim to resolve scope and access before Semester 4. These are suggested preparation steps; your cohort's official milestones may differ.

faq.question: Can I choose any partner university for the thesis?
faq.answer: The programme places the thesis at one of the two universities of your chosen track. Consult the current track route and confirm the host, supervision and registration process before committing to a project.

faq.question: Are these prompts or archived titles available projects?
faq.answer: No. The new prompts are authored examples; archived titles are historical inspiration from an older track structure. Neither is a project offer or an approval. Discuss originality, fit and feasibility with the supervisor and host.

faq.question: Can an internship or external organisation support the thesis?
faq.answer: An external problem can be a useful starting point, and the programme welcomes public or private connections. Clarify academic supervision, independence, access, ownership and confidentiality. An internship is not automatically a thesis, and a commercial report still needs an academic research question.

faq.question: Does public or secondary data mean ethics review is unnecessary?
faq.answer: Do not assume that. Ask your host or faculty to determine the applicable review, exemption and data-protection requirements. Public aggregate indicators and identifiable secondary records raise different issues; decide before relevant data use or recruitment.

faq.question: What if the data or participants never become available?
faq.answer: Tell your supervisor early, document what is unresolved and activate an agreed alternative: a smaller accessible dataset, public-document comparison or appropriately scoped evidence review. Obtain approval for the revised question and method instead of silently changing the project.

faq.question: Must the thesis be quantitative?
faq.answer: Choose a design that answers the question and fits your track, training and supervision. Quantitative, qualitative, modelling and document or evidence-review approaches can address different questions. Confirm that your proposed design meets the actual programme and host requirements.

faq.question: What is the official length or submission deadline?
faq.answer: Use the current joint Thesis Guidelines and your host's instructions. This guide deliberately does not invent a universal word count, form or deadline. Registration, graduation application, thesis upload and defence may have different requirements and dates.

faq.question: May I use generative AI for the thesis?
faq.answer: Check your host's assessment policy and supervisor instructions for the specific use. Obtain clarity about disclosure and prohibited uses; independently verify any output and all citations. Bologna's assessed-work guidance is a host-specific example, not blanket permission across the consortium.

faq.question: What if I find no statistically significant effect?
faq.answer: A careful study can contribute even with null or imprecise results. Report effect sizes, uncertainty, design limitations and what the evidence can support. Do not change outcomes or hide analyses to manufacture a preferred finding.

faq.question: Does completing this hub's checklist count as thesis approval?
faq.answer: No. Saved progress and notes help you organise your work on this device. University approval, ethics decisions, registration and submission happen through official processes. Keep your own backup and avoid entering sensitive research material here.

resources.title: Current thesis rules
resources.description: Starting point for the joint Thesis Guidelines; obtain the current document and your host's instructions.
resources.accessNote: A public overview does not replace cohort-specific guidance sent to students.

resources.title: OECD Health Statistics
resources.description: Compare health spending, resources, service use and outcomes through published indicators and metadata.
resources.accessNote: Primarily aggregate series; verify coverage, definitions and export availability for the exact dataset.

resources.title: Eurostat health database
resources.description: Explore European health status, determinants, care and mortality tables.
resources.accessNote: Public tables do not imply unrestricted survey microdata access; check released breakdowns and metadata.

resources.title: WHO Global Health Observatory
resources.description: Explore international health indicators and their definitions for population-health questions.
resources.accessNote: Some estimates are modelled; confirm source, reference years and uncertainty rather than assuming annual observations.

resources.title: World Bank health data
resources.description: Find cross-country health, nutrition and population indicators with source documentation.
resources.accessNote: Inspect the indicator's underlying source and missingness. Downloadable aggregates are not patient-level records.

resources.title: PRISMA 2020
resources.description: Reporting checklists and flow diagrams for systematic reviews; use the relevant extension for other review types.
resources.accessNote: Reporting guidance supports transparency and does not replace a review protocol or quality appraisal.

resources.title: CHEERS 2022
resources.description: Reporting guidance for health economic evaluations, with attention to assumptions and uncertainty.
resources.accessNote: A reporting checklist is not a model-validation certificate or an official thesis template.

resources.title: EQUATOR guideline library
resources.description: Find reporting guidance appropriate to an observational, qualitative, review or evaluation design.
resources.accessNote: Select a guideline that matches your actual study; confirm relevance with your supervisor.

resources.title: Ethics review: a partner-university example
resources.description: Erasmus explains faculty responsibilities and ethical review; use your own host's route for your project.
resources.accessNote: Procedures vary by faculty and project. Establish the applicable decision before collection or recruitment.

resources.title: AI in assessed work: Bologna guidance
resources.description: A host-specific starting point for permission, verification and disclosure questions.
resources.accessNote: Check current host and supervisor instructions; this does not establish a consortium-wide permission.

resources.title: Erasmus Library literature-search support
resources.description: Learn how to develop a search, select databases and locate full text through university-library support.
resources.accessNote: Subscription access depends on enrolment and library entitlements; use your host's library when access differs.

resources.title: PubMed User Guide
resources.description: Build biomedical searches using concepts, Boolean operators and appropriate filters; record the strategy for a reproducible search.
resources.accessNote: PubMed indexes citations and links to articles; not every indexed article has freely accessible full text.

resources.title: Zotero Quick Start Guide
resources.description: Organise references and notes, export records and insert citations or bibliographies while keeping sources together.
resources.accessNote: Verify imported metadata and citation output; choose the style required by your host or supervisor.
